solution:
**The field at the centre of a circular coil.**

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2r}\)

**Note the factor: it is \(2r\) in the denominator, not \(2\pi r\).** That \(2\pi r\) belongs to the **straight wire** formula; a circular loop at its own centre gives \(\mu_0I/2r\). Mixing the two is the commonest error in this topic, and it would give an answer \(\pi\) times too small.

**Substituting**, with \(r = 4{\cdot}0\) cm \(= 4 \times 10^{-2}\) m:

\(B = \dfrac{\left(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\right)\left(200\right)\left(0{\cdot}40\right)}{2 \times 4 \times 10^{-2}}\)

\(B = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 80}{8 \times 10^{-2}} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{3}\)

\(\boxed{\ B = 4\pi \times 10^{-4} = 1{\cdot}257 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{T} \approx 1{\cdot}3\ \mathrm{mT}\ }\)

**The direction.**

The coil lies in a **horizontal** plane and the current runs **clockwise** when viewed from above. Curl the right hand's fingers in the direction of the current and the thumb gives the field at the centre:

\(\boxed{\ \text{VERTICALLY DOWNWARD, perpendicularly into the horizontal plane}\ }\)

**A quicker way to fix the sense.** A current loop presents a **north** pole to a viewer who sees it running **anticlockwise**, and a **south** pole to one who sees it **clockwise**. Seen from above the current is clockwise, so the upper face is a south pole, and field lines enter a south pole, so inside the coil they point **downward**.

**Why the turns simply multiply.** The \(200\) turns are wound in essentially the same place, each carrying the same current in the same sense, so each contributes the same \(\mu_0I/2r\) and they add. That is why \(N\) appears linearly, and it is how a modest current produces a useful field.

**A sense of the size.** \(1{\cdot}3\) mT is about twenty-five times the Earth's magnetic field \(\left(\approx 5 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}\right)\), enough to swamp it completely, which is why such a coil can be used to deflect a compass needle in a classroom demonstration. Note how little current it takes: \(0{\cdot}40\) A, because the \(200\) turns do the work.

**And note the radius is in the DENOMINATOR.** A smaller coil gives a stronger field at its centre, for the same current and turns, because every part of the winding is closer to the point in question.

(a) From Eq. (4.12)
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}\)
Here, \(N = 100\); \(I = 3.2\,\text{A}\), and \(R = 0.1\,\text{m}\). Hence,
\(B = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 100 \times 3.2}{2 \times 10^{-1}} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-5} \times 10}{2 \times 10^{-1}}\) (using \(\pi \times 3.2 = 10\))
\(= 2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{T}\)
The direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule.
(b) The magnetic moment is given by Eq. (4.24),
\(m = N I A = N I \pi r^{2} = 100 \times 3.2 \times 3.14 \times 10^{-2} = 10\,\text{A m}^{2}\)
The direction is once again given by the right-hand thumb rule.
(c) \(\tau = |\mathbf{m} \times \mathbf{B}|\) [from Eq. (4.23)]
\(= m B \sin\theta\)
Initially, \(\theta = 0\). Thus, initial torque \(\tau_i = 0\). Finally, \(\theta = \pi/2\) (or \(90^{\circ}\)). Thus, final torque \(\tau_f = m B = 10 \times 2 = 20\,\text{N m}\).
(d) From Newton's second law,
\(\mathcal{I}\dfrac{d\omega}{dt} = m B \sin\theta\)
where \(\mathcal{I}\) is the moment of inertia of the coil. From the chain rule,
\(\dfrac{d\omega}{dt} = \dfrac{d\omega}{d\theta}\dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = \dfrac{d\omega}{d\theta}\omega\)
Using this,
\(\mathcal{I}\,\omega\,d\omega = m B \sin\theta\,d\theta\)
Integrating from \(\theta = 0\) to \(\theta = \pi/2\),
\(\mathcal{I}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\omega_f}\omega\,d\omega = m B \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin\theta\,d\theta\)
\(\mathcal{I}\dfrac{\omega_f^{2}}{2} = -m B \cos\theta\Big|_{0}^{\pi/2} = m B\)
\(\omega_f = \left(\dfrac{2mB}{\mathcal{I}}\right)^{1/2} = \left(\dfrac{2 \times 20}{10^{-1}}\right)^{1/2} = 20\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

The proton enters at right angles to the field, so it moves in a circle, and all three parts follow from that.
(a) SPEED. From \(K.E. = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\):
\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times K.E.}{m}}\)
The mass is not given directly but follows from the charge-to-mass ratio: \(m = \dfrac{e}{(q/m)} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{8}} = 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}\).
\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1{\cdot}3384 \times 10^{-14}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-27}}} = 4 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) [with \(m = 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-27}\) kg the root is \(4{\cdot}09 \times 10^{6}\); the given energy is exactly \(\tfrac{1}{2}(1{\cdot}673 \times 10^{-27})(4 \times 10^{6})^{2}\), the proton's true mass, so the question intends \(4 \times 10^{6}\) m/s, as CBSE's scheme uses]
(b) ACCELERATION. The magnetic force supplies the whole of it, and with \(\vec{v}\) perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\):
\(a = \dfrac{qvB}{m} = \left(\dfrac{q}{m}\right)vB = 1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{8} \times 4 \times 10^{6} \times 2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}\)
\(a = 8 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Writing it as \(\left(\dfrac{q}{m}\right)vB\) is what lets the given ratio be used directly.
(c) RADIUS.
\(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{v}{\left(\dfrac{q}{m}\right)B} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{6}}{1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{8} \times 2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}} = 20\ \mathrm{m}\)
The proton travels a circle of radius 20 m. The size is worth noticing: a field of a few millitesla barely curves a proton of this energy, which is why accelerator magnets are measured in tesla rather than millitesla.
note: q/m = 1.0e8 gives m = 1.6e-27 and v = 4.09e6; the energy fits m = 1.673e-27 and v = 4e6, which the scheme uses.

solution:
VECTOR FORM. The Biot-Savart law gives the field contributed by a current element \(I\,d\vec{l}\) at a point whose position vector from the element is \(\vec{r}\):
\(d\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,(d\vec{l} \times \vec{r})}{r^{3}}\)
equivalently, in magnitude,
\(dB = \dfrac{\mu_{0}}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^{2}}\)
where \(\theta\) is the angle between the element and the line joining it to the point.
CALCULATION. The element is at the origin, of length \(dl = 1\ \mathrm{cm} = 10^{-2}\) m, carrying \(I = 10\) A along \(\hat{i}\). The field point is (1 m, 1 m, 0), so
\(\vec{r} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}, \qquad r = \sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2}} = \sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{m}\)
The angle between \(d\vec{l}\), which lies along \(\hat{i}\), and \(\vec{r}\), which lies along the diagonal, is \(45^{\circ}\). Substituting:
\(dB = 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{10 \times 10^{-2} \times \sin 45^{\circ}}{\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^{2}} = 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{10^{-1} \times 0{\cdot}707}{2}\)
\(dB = 3{\cdot}54 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{T}\)
DIRECTION. The field is along \(d\vec{l} \times \vec{r}\), and
\(\hat{i} \times (\hat{i} + \hat{j}) = \hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}\)
so the field points along the POSITIVE z-axis, perpendicular to the plane containing the element and the field point.
The magnitude is about \(3{\cdot}5\) nanotesla, roughly a ten-thousandth of the Earth's field, which is a reminder of how small the contribution of a single short element is.
